claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claims.claim: Benzbromarone-based compounds allosterically inhibit PTP1B by binding to the space normally occupied by the regulatory C-terminal α7 helix.
claims.source: The first class of compounds are based on a benzbromarone (BB) scaffold and inhibit allosterically by binding to the space normally occupied by the regulatory C-terminal α7 helix (Wiesmann et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wiesmann et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Rotations of the α3 helix and a discrete switch of the catalytic WPD loop are impacted by benzbromarone allosteric inhibitors.
claims.source: Recent work combining mutagenesis, X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations revealed how rotations of the α3 helix and a discrete switch of the catalytic WPD loop are impacted by these BB allosteric inhibitors (Choy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Choy et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Benzbromarone molecules were not successfully translated to the clinic.
claims.source: Unfortunately, the BB molecules were not successfully translated to the clinic.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claims.claim: MSI-1436 binds to multiple sites that primarily involve the disordered C-terminus of PTP1B.
claims.source: The second class are natural products, including a molecule called MSI-1436, that bind to multiple sites that primarily involve the disordered C-terminus (Krishnan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krishnan et al., 2014.

claims.claim: MSI-1436 passed Phase I clinical trials but was not advanced to Phase II.
claims.source: MSI-1436 passed Phase I clinical trials but was not advanced to Phase II (Ghattas et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ghattas et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Multitemperature crystallography can reveal previously hidden alternative conformations that enable biological functions.
claims.source: First, multitemperature crystallography (Keedy et al., 2015b) can reveal previously hidden alternative conformations that enable biological functions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Keedy et al., 2015b.

claims.claim: Multitemperature crystallography reveals alternative conformations in PTP1B that are coupled to each other, forming an allosteric network.
claims.source: Here, we use this approach in PTP1B to reveal alternative conformations that are coupled to each other, forming an allosteric network.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The allosteric network in PTP1B includes additional allosteric binding sites that are distinct from the BB site.
claims.source: Moreover, they reveal extensions of this network, including additional allosteric binding sites that are distinct from the BB site (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography data and Figure 1.

claims.claim: High-throughput small-molecule fragment soaking and structure determination has enabled new algorithms for revealing low-occupancy ligands.
claims.source: Second, high-throughput small-molecule fragment soaking and structure determination (Collins et al., 2017) has enabled new algorithms for revealing low-occupancy ligands (Pearce et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2017 and Pearce et al., 2017.

claims.claim: 1627 small-molecule fragments were soaked into PTP1B crystals.
claims.source: We use this approach to comprehensively canvas the PTP1B surface with 1627 small-molecule fragments, 110 of which were structurally resolved in complex with PTP1B.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text and supported by the fragment screening experiments.

claims.claim: 110 small-molecule fragments were structurally resolved in complex with PTP1B.
claims.source: We use this approach to comprehensively canvas the PTP1B surface with 1627 small-molecule fragments, 110 of which were structurally resolved in complex with PTP1B.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text and supported by the fragment screening experiments.

claims.claim: The fragments cluster into 11 fragment-binding hotspots outside of the active site.
claims.source: The fragments cluster into 11 fragment-binding hotspots outside of the active site.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text and supported by the fragment screening data.

claims.claim: Fragment-binding sites that are conformationally coupled to the active site based on multitemperature crystallography bound more fragments than any other sites.
claims.source: Strikingly, the sites chosen in this way bound more fragments than did any other sites -- suggesting that conformational heterogeneity may be important for both allostery and ligand binding.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the convergence of multitemperature crystallography and fragment screening data.

claims.claim: Conformational heterogeneity may be important for both allostery and ligand binding in PTP1B.
claims.source: Strikingly, the sites chosen in this way bound more fragments than did any other sites -- suggesting that conformational heterogeneity may be important for both allostery and ligand binding.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that conformationally coupled sites bind more fragments.

claims.claim: Covalently tethered small molecules at one allosteric site allosterically inhibit PTP1B enzyme activity.
claims.source: Finally, we use covalently tethered small molecules (Erlanson et al., 2004) at one of these sites to confirm that it is functionally linked to enzyme activity, thereby supporting our predictions from multitemperature crystallography of the apo protein.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the covalent tethering experiments and enzyme activity assays described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Transition of the WPD loop from the open to the closed state is rate-limiting for catalysis in PTP1B.
claims.source: Transition of this loop from the open to the closed state is rate-limiting for catalysis (Whittier et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whittier et al., 2013.

claims.claim: In the only available apo crystal structure of PTP1B in which the WPD loop is free from crystal-lattice contacts (PDB ID 1sug), the loop is modeled in the closed state.
claims.source: In the only available apo crystal structure of PTP1B in which the WPD loop is free from crystal-lattice contacts (PDB ID 1sug) (Pedersen et al., 2004), the loop is modeled in the closed state.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pedersen et al., 2004 and reference to PDB ID 1sug.

claims.claim: Low-contour electron density can reveal hidden alternative conformations in protein crystal structures.
claims.source: However, low-contour electron density can reveal hidden alternative conformations in protein crystal structures (Lang et al., 2010; Fraser et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lang et al., 2010 and Fraser et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The electron density in the apo structure of PTP1B (PDB ID 1sug) suggests a significant population for the open state of the WPD loop as well as the closed state.
claims.source: Surprisingly, upon closer inspection, the electron density strongly suggests a significant population for the open state as well (Figure 2C, left).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the electron density analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: A re-refined model with both open and closed states of the WPD loop as alternative conformations visually accounts for the electron density around this loop much better than the original model.
claims.source: Our re-refined model with both open and closed states as alternative conformations visually accounts for the electron density around this loop much better than the original model (Figure 2C, left).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the re-refinement analysis and Figure 2C.

claims.claim: When 36 other available crystal structures of PTP1B complexed with active-site inhibitors were re-refined using both open and closed loop states as putative alternative conformations, Fo-Fc difference electron density and the bimodal distribution of refined occupancies indicated the single-state models were a better fit.
claims.source: By contrast, when we re-refined 36 other available crystal structures of PTP1B complexed with active-site inhibitors using both open and closed loop states as putative alternative conformations, Fo-Fc difference electron density and the bimodal distribution of refined occupancies indicated the single-state models were a better fit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the re-refinement analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Apo PTP1B samples both WPD loop states even in the crystal.
claims.source: These results suggest that, even in the crystal, apo PTP1B samples both WPD loop states and that active-site inhibitors then lock the loop either fully open or fully closed.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the re-refinement analysis of apo and inhibitor-bound structures.

claims.claim: Active-site inhibitors lock the WPD loop either fully open or fully closed.
claims.source: These results suggest that, even in the crystal, apo PTP1B samples both WPD loop states and that active-site inhibitors then lock the loop either fully open or fully closed.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the re-refinement analysis of apo and inhibitor-bound structures.

claims.claim: X-ray datasets of apo PTP1B were collected at 100 K, 180 K, 240 K, and 278 K, all at better than 2 Å resolution.
claims.source: To better characterize the conformational heterogeneity of the WPD loop in apo PTP1B, we collected X-ray datasets at several elevated temperatures including 180 K, 240 K, and 278 K ('room temperature') in addition to the 100 K ('cryogenic') model from the PDB, all at better than 2 Å resolution (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data collection described in the text and Table 1.

claims.claim: Each complete multitemperature dataset was obtained from a single crystal.
claims.source: Each complete dataset was obtained from a single crystal, and crystallographic statistics indicated that radiation damage was not a concern even at the elevated temperatures (Diederichs, 2006) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Radiation damage was not a concern even at the elevated temperatures for the multitemperature datasets.
claims.source: Each complete dataset was obtained from a single crystal, and crystallographic statistics indicated that radiation damage was not a concern even at the elevated temperatures (Diederichs, 2006) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the crystallographic statistics and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, with a citation to Diederichs, 2006.

claims.claim: The occupancy of the open conformation of the WPD loop increases non-linearly with temperature.
claims.source: The WPD loop adopts both the open and closed conformations across this range (Figure 2C) and the population of the open vs. closed states was sensitive to temperature (Figure 2D). The loop is approximately 67% closed at 100 K, but 65% open at 278 K. These occupancies evolve non-linearly (Keedy et al., 2015b) at intermediate temperatures.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to Keedy et al., 2015b.

claims.claim: The WPD loop is approximately 67% closed at 100 K.
claims.source: The loop is approximately 67% closed at 100 K, but 65% open at 278 K.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the occupancy refinement data from the multitemperature structures.

claims.claim: The WPD loop is 65% open at 278 K.
claims.source: The loop is approximately 67% closed at 100 K, but 65% open at 278 K.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the occupancy refinement data from the multitemperature structures.

claims.claim: Temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity was observed for several other regions of PTP1B, including the BB allosteric site, the '197 site', and the 'loop 16 (L16) site'.
claims.source: Overall, we also observed temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity for several other regions of PTP1B, including the previously characterized BB allosteric site, plus additional sites we refer to as the '197 site' and the 'loop 16 (L16) site'.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography data described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The BB allosteric site, the 197 site, and the L16 site are all contiguous in the structure of PTP1B.
claims.source: These regions are all contiguous in the structure (Figure 2E), suggesting that they together constitute an expanded collective allosteric network in PTP1B that is coupled to the WPD loop.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The BB allosteric site, the 197 site, and the L16 site together constitute an expanded collective allosteric network in PTP1B that is coupled to the WPD loop.
claims.source: These regions are all contiguous in the structure (Figure 2E), suggesting that they together constitute an expanded collective allosteric network in PTP1B that is coupled to the WPD loop.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural contiguity and conformational coupling observed in the multitemperature data.

claims.claim: BB2 binds to an allosteric site >12 Å away from the active site and inhibits enzyme activity.
claims.source: To connect these multitemperature structures to known allosteric regulatory mechanisms, we first turned to a benzbromarone derivative compound (here referred to as BB2) that binds to an allosteric site >12 Å away from the active site and inhibits enzyme activity (Wiesmann et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wiesmann et al., 2004.

claims.claim: BB2 directly displaces Trp291 to disorder the entire C-terminal α7 helix.
claims.source: The authors of the study reporting BB2 described a series of induced conformational changes that begins with BB2 directly displacing Trp291 to disorder the entire C-terminal α7 helix, and ends with Phe191 χ2 dihedral-angle rotations clashing with the WPD loop anchor residue Trp179 to stabilize the open state.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description from the study by Wiesmann et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Phe191 χ2 dihedral-angle rotations clash with the WPD loop anchor residue Trp179 to stabilize the open state.
claims.source: The authors of the study reporting BB2 described a series of induced conformational changes that begins with BB2 directly displacing Trp291 to disorder the entire C-terminal α7 helix, and ends with Phe191 χ2 dihedral-angle rotations clashing with the WPD loop anchor residue Trp179 to stabilize the open state.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description from the study by Wiesmann et al., 2004.

claims.claim: In apo PTP1B, the α7 helix is more ordered at lower temperatures but more disordered at higher temperatures.
claims.source: Indeed, in apo PTP1B the α7 helix is more ordered at lower temperatures but more disordered at higher temperatures (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Trp179 and Phe191 adopt dual conformations at higher temperatures in apo PTP1B.
claims.source: Also, Trp179 and Phe191 adopt dual conformations at higher temperatures (Figure 3B) that coincide well with the apo and allosterically inhibited conformations (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The dual conformations of Trp179 and Phe191 at higher temperatures coincide well with the apo and allosterically inhibited conformations.
claims.source: Also, Trp179 and Phe191 adopt dual conformations at higher temperatures (Figure 3B) that coincide well with the apo and allosterically inhibited conformations (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Alternative conformations at high temperatures are observed for several residues within and directly flanking the WPD loop (Arg221, Pro185, Trp179, Phe269) which have been implicated as being important for a CH/π switch during WPD loop opening/closing.
claims.source: We also see alternative conformations at high temperatures for several residues within and directly flanking the WPD loop (Arg221, Pro185, Trp179, Phe269) which have been implicated as being important for a CH/π switch during WPD loop opening/closing (Choy et al., 2017) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Choy et al., 2017.

claims.claim: BB2 stabilizes a subset of pre-existing conformations in apo PTP1B.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that BB2 stabilizes a subset of pre-existing conformations in apo PTP1B.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that conformations seen with BB2 are also present in apo PTP1B at higher temperatures.

claims.claim: A high-resolution (1.80 Å) structure of PTP1B in complex with BB3 was solved at 273 K.
claims.source: We additionally solved a high-resolution (1.80 Å, Table 1) structure of PTP1B in complex with BB3 (which differs from BB2 only by an extra terminal aminothiazole group) at 273 K and found it to be very similar to the 100 K structures with BB3 (PDB ID 1t4j) and with BB2 (PDB ID 1t49) despite the difference in temperature (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data collection and structure determination described in the text and Table 1.

claims.claim: The structure of PTP1B in complex with BB3 at 273 K is very similar to the 100 K structures with BB3 (PDB ID 1t4j) and with BB2 (PDB ID 1t49) despite the difference in temperature.
claims.source: We additionally solved a high-resolution (1.80 Å, Table 1) structure of PTP1B in complex with BB3 (which differs from BB2 only by an extra terminal aminothiazole group) at 273 K and found it to be very similar to the 100 K structures with BB3 (PDB ID 1t4j) and with BB2 (PDB ID 1t49) despite the difference in temperature (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: At 273 K but not at 100 K, modeling BB3 with a single conformer leads to Fo-Fc difference electron density peaks at both ends of the molecule.
claims.source: First, at 273 K but not at 100 K, modeling BB3 with a single conformer leads to Fo-Fc difference electron density peaks at both ends of the molecule (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the electron density analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Adding a second alternative conformer to the BB3 model accounts for the Fo-Fc difference electron density peaks.
claims.source: To account for these peaks in the map, it is necessary to add a second alternative conformer to the model, which includes a translation at one end and dihedral-angle changes at the other end (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: At 273 K, significant electron density is observed just above BB3 in the PTP1B structure.
claims.source: Second, at 273 K, we observe significant electron density just above BB3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the electron density analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Modeling a reordered, non-helical conformation of α7 explains the electron density above BB3 at 273 K.
claims.source: Modeling a reordered, non-helical conformation of α7 explains this density well, and places Trp291 in good position for aromatic stacking interactions with BB3 and other interactions with nearby sidechains on the α3 helix (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: Trp291 is displaced by BB3 or BB2 binding in a striking example of molecular mimicry.
claims.source: Trp291 is displaced by BB3 or BB2 binding in a striking example of molecular mimicry (Wiesmann et al., 2004) (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wiesmann et al., 2004 and the structural analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: A subsequent reordering of the α7 polypeptide occurs after BB3 binding, which may contribute to the affinity of BB3 for PTP1B.
claims.source: Our 273 K data suggest that a subsequent reordering of the α7 polypeptide occurs, which may contribute to the affinity of BB3 for PTP1B.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the electron density analysis at 273 K.

claims.claim: In the 100 K structure with BB1, α7 reorders but adopts a significantly different conformation than observed at 273 K with BB3.
claims.source: However, in the 100 K structure with BB1, a different derivative of the BB scaffold, α7 also reorders -- but adopts a significantly different conformation than we observe at 273 K with BB3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E,G.

claims.claim: α7 is quite malleable when disordered, and may interact in diverse ways with bound ligands.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that in addition to being a major allosteric hub when ordered (Choy et al., 2017), α7 is also quite malleable when disordered, and may interact in diverse ways with bound ligands -- behavior which is similar to the mechanism proposed for inhibitors that bind via the disordered C-terminus beyond α7 (Krishnan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural observations of α7 in different conditions and supported by citations to Choy et al., 2017 and Krishnan et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Temperature-dependent ordering was observed in loop 16 (L16; residues 237–243) that sits underneath the α6-α7 junction.
claims.source: We also observed temperature-dependent ordering in a loop (loop 16, L16; residues 237–243) that sits underneath the α6-α7 junction just beyond the BB binding site.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography data described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The electron density for L16 at higher temperature clearly reveals an alternative conformation with its backbone shifted by >5 Å from the primary conformation.
claims.source: By contrast to lower temperature (Figure 4A), the electron density for L16 at higher temperature (Figure 4B) clearly reveals an alternative conformation with its backbone shifted by >5 Å from the primary conformation (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the electron density analysis shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claims.claim: The L16 alternative conformation sampled by apo PTP1B matches the L16 conformation when PTP1B is allosterically inhibited by BB2.
claims.source: Remarkably, this L16 alternative conformation sampled by apo PTP1B matches the L16 conformation when PTP1B is allosterically inhibited by BB2 (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: BB2 selects pre-existing, globally dispersed conformations rather than inducing new ones.
claims.source: This rearrangement provides further evidence that BB2 selects pre-existing, globally dispersed conformations rather than inducing new ones.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the L16 conformation with BB2 is already present in apo PTP1B.

claims.claim: The L16 site is seemingly coupled to the α6 helix.
claims.source: The L16 site is seemingly coupled to the α6 helix: Lys239 from L16 H-bonds with Ile281 from α6 in the global closed state, but not in the global open state in which L16 adopts its alternative conformation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural analysis of hydrogen bonding patterns.

claims.claim: The L16 site is a component of the collective allosteric network in PTP1B.
claims.source: Because α6 is directly coupled to the α7 order-disorder transition, we therefore propose that the L16 site is a component of the collective allosteric network in PTP1B.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural coupling between L16, α6, and α7.

claims.claim: Several residues lining the L16 site (including Met3, Lys237, and Ser242) were included in a region called 'Cluster II', which was suggested to be a previously unidentified allosteric site based on reciprocal NMR chemical shift perturbations.
claims.source: However, in a more recent study, several residues lining what we call the L16 site (including Met3, Lys237, and Ser242) were included in a region called 'Cluster II', which was suggested to be a previously unidentified allosteric site based on reciprocal NMR chemical shift perturbations upon mutation of this site or the WPD loop (Cui et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Multitemperature crystallography complements NMR findings by independently identifying the L16 allosteric site using a new methodology.
claims.source: Our work here using multitemperature crystallography complements these findings by independently identifying this allosteric site using a new methodology, and by revealing in atomic detail how multiple conformational states at the L16 site may aid communication with the active site.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the convergence of multitemperature crystallography and NMR data.

claims.claim: The L16 site may be not only energetically coupled to the active site, but also capable of forming an under-appreciated small-molecule binding pocket via conformational heterogeneity.
claims.source: Therefore, the L16 site may be not only energetically coupled to the active site, but also capable of forming an under-appreciated small-molecule binding pocket via the conformational heterogeneity we observe.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the conformational heterogeneity observed at the L16 site and supported by a citation to Cimermancic et al., 2016a.

claims.claim: Residues with temperature-sensitive conformational heterogeneity were observed in the '197 site'.
claims.source: In addition to the temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity observed at the BB site and L16 site, we observed residues with temperature-sensitive conformational heterogeneity in the '197 site' (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the multitemperature crystallography data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The alternative conformations of several residues in the 197 site have a pattern of steric incompatibility with multiple states of the WPD loop and α7 helix.
claims.source: Moreover, the alternative conformations of several residues in this region have a pattern of steric incompatibility with multiple states of the WPD loop and α7 helix, suggesting that the 197 site may be mechanistically linked to the active site in a similar way as the BB binding site.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural analysis of steric clashes.

claims.claim: A major link between the WPD loop and the 197 site is Tyr152.
claims.source: A major link between the WPD loop and the 197 site is Tyr152.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the structural analysis of Tyr152 conformations.

claims.claim: When the WPD loop is closed and the α7 helix is ordered, Tyr152 adopts a 'down rotamer'.
claims.source: When the WPD loop is closed and the α7 helix is ordered, Tyr152 adopts a 'down rotamer' (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, red).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: When the WPD loop is open and the α7 helix is disordered, the 278 K electron density suggests that Tyr152 adopts an 'up rotamer'.
claims.source: By contrast, when the WPD loop is open and the α7 helix is disordered, the 278 K electron density suggests that Tyr152 adopts an 'up rotamer' (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, orange).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the electron density analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The down rotamer of Tyr152 is sterically incompatible with phosphorylation of Tyr152.
claims.source: The down rotamer is sterically incompatible with phosphorylation of Tyr152, which occurs in vivo (Bandyopadhyay et al., 1997; Rhee et al., 2001), suggesting that the up rotamer may have additional regulatory roles.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural analysis and supported by citations to Bandyopadhyay et al., 1997 and Rhee et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Tyr152 is phosphorylated in vivo.
claims.source: The down rotamer is sterically incompatible with phosphorylation of Tyr152, which occurs in vivo (Bandyopadhyay et al., 1997; Rhee et al., 2001), suggesting that the up rotamer may have additional regulatory roles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bandyopadhyay et al., 1997 and Rhee et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Tyr152 in the L11 backbone conformation with just the down rotamer is sterically incompatible with the open WPD loop conformation.
claims.source: Tyr152 in the L11 backbone conformation with just the down rotamer (red in Figure 5—figure supplement 1) is sterically incompatible with the open WPD loop conformation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The Tyr152 up rotamer is sterically incompatible with the ordered α7 conformation.
claims.source: Similarly, the Tyr152 up rotamer is sterically incompatible with the ordered α7 conformation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The allosteric circuitry of PTP1B involving Tyr152 is complex and multibody.
claims.source: These results together suggest that the allosteric circuitry of PTP1B involving Tyr152 is complex and multibody.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural analysis of Tyr152 conformations and their steric incompatibilities.

claims.claim: Tyr152 likely exemplifies a population shuffling mechanism whereby mixtures of microstates (rotameric state of Tyr152) exchange on a fast timescale as the protein transitions between macrostates (WPD loop state, α7 ordering, and L11 backbone shifting) on a slower timescale.
claims.source: Tyr152 likely exemplifies a population shuffling mechanism whereby mixtures of microstates (rotameric state of Tyr152) exchange on a fast timescale as the protein transitions between macrostates (WPD loop state, α7 ordering, and L11 backbone shifting) on a slower timescale (Smith et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural analysis and supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The electron density suggests a complex interplay between alternative conformations for Asn193 on the α3 helix and Tyr152 on loop 11 (L11) at temperatures above 100 K.
claims.source: In our datasets at temperatures above 100 K, the electron density suggests a complex interplay between alternative conformations for Asn193 on the α3 helix and Tyr152 on loop 11 (L11) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the electron density analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The N-terminal region of the α3 helix (through Phe196) rotates by 2–20°, resulting in shifts of 0.2–0.7 Å for some Cα atoms, based on 100 K crystal structures of apo (WPD-open) vs. active-site-inhibitor-bound (WPD-closed) PTP1B.
claims.source: The N-terminal region of this helix (through Phe196) rotates by 2–20°, resulting in shifts of 0.2–0.7 Å for some Cα atoms, based on 100 K crystal structures of apo (WPD-open) vs. active-site-inhibitor-bound (WPD-closed) PTP1B (Choy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Choy et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The multiconformer model for the 278 K apo dataset includes alternative backbone conformations for the WPD loop and the beginning of α3, through Asn193 plus Phe196-Lys197.
claims.source: Similarly, the multiconformer model for our 278 K apo dataset includes alternative backbone conformations for the WPD loop and the beginning of α3, through Asn193 plus Phe196-Lys197 (this is a conservative interpretation of which residues in the helix have alternative backbone conformations).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling of the 278 K apo structure.

claims.claim: α3 inherently shifts as the protein transitions between its global macrostates, even in the apo state.
claims.source: Our results suggest that α3 inherently shifts as the protein transitions betweens its global macrostates, even in the apo state.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of alternative backbone conformations in the apo structure.

claims.claim: Several residues propagating down L11 from Tyr152, and down α3 from Asn193, also adopt multiple conformations at higher temperatures.
claims.source: Strikingly, several residues propagating down L11 from Tyr152, and down α3 from Asn193, also adopt multiple conformations at higher temperatures (Figure 5).

claims.claim: Regulatory domains or subdomains were recently targeted for allosteric inhibition of the serine/threonine phosphatases Wip1 and PP1.
claims.source: Similarly, regulatory domains or subdomains were recently targeted for allosteric inhibition of the serine/threonine phosphatases Wip1 (Gilmartin et al., 2014) and PP1 (Carrara et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gilmartin et al., 2014 and Carrara et al., 2017.

results.result: PTP1B is a validated therapeutic target for diabetes, cancer, and Rett syndrome, but no active-site inhibitors have reached clinical use due to issues with specificity and bioavailability. Two classes of allosteric inhibitors (benzbromarone-based and MSI-1436) have been developed but neither successfully translated to the clinic.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 establish the therapeutic importance of PTP1B and the challenges with existing inhibitor approaches. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Elchebly 1999, Krishnan 2014/2015, Wiesmann 2004, Ghattas 2016). This provides essential context for why new allosteric approaches are needed.

results.result: Re-analysis of the published apo PTP1B structure (PDB 1sug) reveals that the WPD loop samples both open and closed conformations in the crystal, contrary to the original single-conformation model. Active-site inhibitors lock the loop into either fully open or fully closed states.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C30 demonstrate through re-refinement analysis that low-contour electron density supports dual WPD loop conformations in apo PTP1B (C26-C27), while inhibitor-bound structures show single conformations (C28). This is a key finding that challenges the original interpretation and is well-supported by crystallographic data (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Multitemperature X-ray crystallography of apo PTP1B at 100K, 180K, 240K, and 278K reveals that the WPD loop occupancy shifts non-linearly from 67% closed at 100K to 65% open at 278K, with no significant radiation damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 present high-quality multitemperature crystallographic data (Table 1, Figure 2C-D) showing temperature-dependent conformational changes. The single-crystal approach (C32) and radiation damage assessment (C33) strengthen confidence in the results. The non-linear temperature dependence (C34) is appropriately cited to prior work (Keedy 2015b).

results.result: Multitemperature crystallography reveals an expanded allosteric network in PTP1B comprising the BB site, the 197 site, and the L16 site, all contiguous on the 'back side' of the protein and conformationally coupled to the WPD loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39, C14-C15, C100-C101, and C192 collectively establish the existence of a large allosteric network. The structural contiguity (C38, Figure 2E) and conformational coupling (C39, C85) are demonstrated through multitemperature data. This represents a major extension of previously known allosteric sites.

results.result: The benzbromarone allosteric inhibitor BB2 stabilizes pre-existing conformations in apo PTP1B rather than inducing new ones. At higher temperatures, apo PTP1B samples conformations of the α7 helix, Trp179, and Phe191 that match those seen with BB2 binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C47 demonstrate conformational selection rather than induced fit for BB2 inhibition. The multitemperature data (C43-C45, Figure 3A-C) show that conformations observed with BB2 pre-exist in apo protein at elevated temperatures. This mechanistic insight is well-supported by structural comparisons and appropriately cites prior work (Wiesmann 2004, Choy 2017).

results.result: High-resolution structure of PTP1B with BB3 at 273K reveals conformational heterogeneity of the inhibitor and reordering of the α7 helix into a non-helical conformation that interacts with BB3. The α7 helix is malleable when disordered and can adopt different conformations with different ligands.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C57 present novel structural insights into BB3 binding at elevated temperature. The electron density analysis (C50-C53, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) clearly supports alternative conformations of both BB3 and α7. The comparison with BB1 (C56) demonstrates ligand-dependent α7 conformations. This extends understanding of the BB allosteric mechanism.

results.result: Loop 16 (L16) undergoes temperature-dependent conformational changes with backbone shifts >5Å. The alternative L16 conformation in apo PTP1B matches that seen with BB2 inhibition, and the site is coupled to the α6 helix and α7 order-disorder transition, making it part of the allosteric network.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 establish L16 as a novel allosteric site through multitemperature crystallography (C59, Figure 4B-D) and structural coupling analysis (C62). Claims C64-C65 appropriately cite convergent NMR evidence (Cui 2017). The inference that L16 is part of the allosteric network (C63) is well-supported by the structural coupling data. Claim C66 about ligandability is more speculative but reasonably inferred.

results.result: The 197 site shows temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity with steric incompatibilities linking it to WPD loop and α7 helix states. Tyr152 adopts different rotamers coupled to WPD loop states, and the α3 helix undergoes subtle backbone shifts. Multiple residues in this region show coordinated conformational changes with similar temperature dependence to the WPD loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C85 comprehensively characterize the 197 site through multitemperature crystallography. The steric incompatibility analysis (C68, C74-C75) and temperature-dependent occupancy changes (C84-C85, Figure 5A) provide strong evidence for allosteric coupling. The complex conformational behavior of Tyr152 (C69-C77) is well-documented with electron density (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The population shuffling mechanism (C77) is appropriately cited to prior work (Smith 2015).

results.result: The 197 site has been independently implicated as allosteric by prior NMR and mutagenesis studies. Ordered glycerols and MPD bind to this site in crystal structures, suggesting it may be bindable by other small molecules and capable of propagating conformational changes to the WPD loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 appropriately cite convergent evidence from prior studies (Cui 2017, Choy 2017). Claims C90-C92 document fortuitous ligand binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), supporting ligandability. Claim C93 is a reasonable hypothesis based on the conformational coupling data, though it requires experimental validation.

results.result: Point mutations at the 197 site (Y152G, Y153A, K197A) reduce PTP1B catalytic efficiency, with effects correlating with distance from the WPD loop. This demonstrates that local perturbations at the 197 site can impact catalysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 present mutagenesis data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) showing that all three mutations reduce kcat/KM, with a distance-dependent effect (C97-C98). This provides functional validation that the 197 site is allosterically linked to catalysis. The data quality appears adequate with error bars shown.

results.result: Tyr176 in the hydrophobic core adopts alternative conformations at higher temperatures that are structurally compatible with different conformations of surface-exposed Tyr152 and buried Trp179, potentially linking the 197 site to the WPD loop through coordinated hydrophobic shifts.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 describe a mechanistic link through the protein core (Figure 5—figure supplement 4). The structural analysis is well-documented and appropriately cites prior work on rotamer preferences (Lovell 2000) and allosteric pathways (Choy 2017, Cui 2017, Wiesmann 2004). This provides molecular detail on how surface and buried residues communicate.

results.result: High-throughput fragment screening was performed by soaking 1918 apo PTP1B crystals with small-molecule fragments and 48 with DMSO. Of 1774 successfully processed datasets (average resolution 2.1Å), 110 fragment hits were confidently modeled after PanDDA analysis revealed 381 putative binding events.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C111, C17-C18 describe a large-scale fragment screening campaign. The numbers are clearly stated and the data quality is high (65% better than 2.0Å resolution). The PanDDA approach (C112-C115) for identifying low-occupancy ligands is appropriately cited (Pearce 2017, Collins 2017). The manual inspection step (C115) adds rigor.

results.result: The 110 fragment hits cluster into 12 structurally distinct binding sites (11 outside the active site) that are widely distributed across the PTP1B surface. Twenty-five fragments bind to multiple sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 and C19 characterize the fragment binding sites. The structural distinctness criterion (C117) is clearly defined. The distribution across the surface (C118, Figure 6E) and promiscuous binding (C119) are appropriately noted. This provides a comprehensive map of ligandable sites.

results.result: Twenty-four fragments bind to the BB allosteric site, with many overlapping the BB scaffold but also extending in new directions. One structure shows the α7 helix adopting a reordered conformation covering the binding site. This validates that fragment screening can identify allosteric sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 demonstrate retrospective validation of the fragment screening approach (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The convergence with the known BB site (C125-C126) and novel extensions (C127) provide both validation and new chemical matter. The reordered α7 observation (C129) adds structural insight.

results.result: The L16 site and 197 site are fragment-binding hotspots with 17 and 30 fragments respectively. These sites identified by multitemperature crystallography as allosterically coupled bound more fragments than any other sites, suggesting conformational heterogeneity is important for both allostery and ligand binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C133, C20-C21 demonstrate striking convergence between two independent methods (Figure 7B-C). The observation that conformationally coupled sites are the most ligandable (C20) is a key finding. However, the inference about conformational heterogeneity being important for binding (C21, C202) is somewhat speculative and could benefit from additional analysis.

results.result: Most fragments at the L16 site appear to pry apart loop 16, α1, and α6 to create a cryptic binding site. The fragments share common features including aromatic moieties sandwiching between Pro239 and Met282, and do not overlap with BB site fragments.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 characterize L16 fragment binding (Figure 7B). The cryptic site interpretation (C134) is appropriately cited (Cimermancic 2016a). The common binding features (C135) and distinctness from BB site (C136) are supported by structural analysis.

results.result: Thirty fragments bind to the 197 site in two subsites separated by a ridge. Fragments are characterized by aromatic packing above Leu172 and do not overlap with BB site fragments, but several overlap with ordered glycerols from multitemperature structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 characterize 197 site fragment binding (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The two-subsite architecture (C137) and binding features (C138) are clearly described. The overlap with glycerols (C140) provides additional validation and is appropriately discussed with citation (Mattos and Ringe 1996).

results.result: Ensemble structures of fragment-bound PTP1B show subtle structural differences (0.7-1.7Å backbone RMSD) between ground and bound states. Fragment binding did not dramatically shift the WPD loop from open to closed, likely due to absence of glycerol, and weak fragments elicit primarily local conformational changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C149 analyze global conformational effects of fragment binding. The ensemble modeling approach (C144) is innovative. The small RMSD values (C145) and lack of dramatic WPD loop shifts (C147) are honestly reported. The interpretation about glycerol absence (C148) and weak fragment effects (C149) are reasonable inferences from the data.

results.result: Twenty fragments predicted to bind the 197 or L16 sites showed no inhibition of enzyme activity up to maximum assayable concentrations. This lack of inhibition is unsurprising given the fragments' small sizes, simple structures, and low affinities (10-30% occupancy at 30-150mM).
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C153 report negative results from fragment activity assays. The lack of inhibition (C151) is appropriately contextualized by the low occupancies (C153) and fragment properties (C152). This honest reporting of negative results strengthens the overall manuscript and appropriately sets expectations for fragment hits.

results.result: Tethering screening of 1600 disulfide fragments against K197C identified 50 hits, with fragment 1 showing correlated tethering and inhibition. Compound 2, designed with a reversed amide bond, showed improved tethering and inhibition of K197C relative to compound 1.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C165 describe the tethering screen and hit optimization (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The screen size (C161) and hit identification (C162-C163) are clearly documented. The rational design of compound 2 (C164) and improved properties (C165) demonstrate successful optimization. The tethering method is appropriately cited (Kathman 2014, Burlingame 2011).

results.result: Compound 2 exhibits dose-dependent tethering (EC50 = 7.8±1.1 µM) and partial noncompetitive allosteric inhibition of K197C (Ki = 7.1±1.1 µM, ~60% max inhibition) with ~50% reduction in Vmax but no effect on KM. Compound 2 shows minimal tethering and inhibition of WT*, supporting specificity for the 197 site.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C169 present comprehensive kinetic characterization (Figure 8B-C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2). The dose-response curves, Michaelis-Menten analysis, and WT* control experiments provide strong evidence for specific, noncompetitive allosteric inhibition. The similar EC50 and Ki values (C166) support a direct relationship between tethering and inhibition.

results.result: The K197C-2 tethered complex shows inhibition with the alternative substrate DiFMUP, with dramatic reduction in Vmax but no significant effect on KM, further supporting a noncompetitive allosteric mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claim C170 provides orthogonal validation using a different substrate (Figure 8—figure supplement 3). The consistent kinetic pattern (reduced Vmax, unchanged KM) across two substrates strengthens the mechanistic conclusion. The DiFMUP assay is appropriately cited (Welte 2005).

results.result: High-resolution crystal structure (1.95Å) of K197C tethered with 2 confirms binding to the 197 site rather than the active site or BB site. The 83% refined occupancy matches ~85% conjugation measured in solution. Compound 2 adopts a nearly coplanar conformation and packs against Leu172, with several noncovalent fragments overlaying well with the tethered compound.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C177 provide structural validation of the tethering results (Figure 9A-B, Table 1). The site confirmation (C172-C173) rules out off-target binding. The occupancy agreement (C174) validates the modeling. The structural convergence with fragments (C177) is particularly compelling and supports future medicinal chemistry efforts.

results.result: Tethering of 2 to K197C induces conformational changes in the α3 helix (backbone shift, N193 rotamer switch, F196/E200 movements) and α6 helix (E276, F280) that mirror changes from open-to-closed apo PTP1B. This suggests allosteric inhibition involves conformational changes similar to the global open-to-closed transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C182 analyze conformational changes upon tethering (Figure 9C-D). The structural comparisons are well-documented and appropriately cite prior work (Choy 2017). Claim C183 provides convergent evidence from mutagenesis (Cui 2017). The mechanistic interpretation (C182, C184) is reasonable but acknowledges remaining uncertainties.

results.result: The percent tethering of compound 2 correlates with percent inhibition, but maximum inhibition is only ~60%, consistent with partial noncompetitive allosteric inhibition. Kinetic analysis shows reduction in Vmax without change in KM, a common paradigm in noncompetitive allosteric inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C207-C210 integrate the tethering and kinetic data. The correlation (C207) supports a direct mechanism. The partial inhibition (C208) and kinetic pattern (C209) are well-documented. The contextualization with general principles (C210) is appropriately cited (Ramsay and Tipton 2017, Whiteley 2000).

results.result: The study uses two complementary approaches: multitemperature crystallography to reveal conformationally coupled alternative conformations forming an allosteric network, and high-throughput fragment screening with PanDDA analysis to identify ligandable sites. En masse structural analysis reveals minor conformations and shifts that enable protein function.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15, C186, C189-C191 describe the overall methodological approach. Both methods are appropriately cited (Keedy 2015b, Collins 2017, Pearce 2017). The complementary nature of the approaches and their convergence on the same sites is a key strength of the study.

results.result: Multitemperature crystallography reveals in atomic detail the alternative conformations that the 197 and L16 sites natively populate. The work suggests allosteric perturbations stabilize pre-existing conformations rather than inducing new ones. Allostery in PTP1B involves interdependent conformational changes spanning multiple length scales.
results.evaluation: Claims C195-C197 synthesize key mechanistic insights. The conformational selection model (C196) is well-supported by the multitemperature data showing that inhibitor-bound conformations pre-exist in apo protein. The multi-scale nature of allostery (C197) is demonstrated throughout the structural analysis.

results.result: Multitemperature X-ray analysis of apo protein provides a way to predict allosterically coupled binding sites. The convergence of allosteric coupling and ligandability on the same sites suggests conformational changes may be important for allosteric ligand binding in PTP1B.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C202 present a key conceptual advance. The convergence of independent methods (C201) is striking and well-documented. However, the inference about conformational heterogeneity being important for binding (C202) is somewhat speculative - the correlation is clear but causation is not definitively established. Additional experiments could strengthen this claim.

results.result: The cocrystal structures with fragments bound at the 197, L16, and BB sites, combined with the tethered inhibitor structure showing convergence with fragment poses, offer a foothold for future medicinal chemistry efforts to design allosteric inhibitors for PTP1B.
results.evaluation: Claims C154, C178, C205 discuss future applications. The structural convergence between fragments and tethered compound 2 (C178, Figure 9B) is particularly compelling. The claim about enabling future drug design (C154, C205) is reasonable given the extensive structural information provided, though actual drug development success remains to be demonstrated.

results.result: The druggability of the 197 site in WT PTP1B is supported by recent computational work showing it bound diverse molecules in silico and was most responsive to allosteric perturbations among potential allosteric pockets.
results.evaluation: Claim C211 cites convergent computational evidence (Kumar 2018) supporting the 197 site as druggable. This external validation strengthens the experimental findings, though the computational predictions still require experimental validation in WT protein.

results.result: The allosteric network revealed by in vitro perturbations may be relevant to in vivo regulation through: (1) C-terminal phosphorylation and protein interactions, (2) Tyr152 phosphorylation affecting IRK and cadherin binding, and (3) protein-protein interactions on the 'back side' observed in other PTPs. The network may function as a 'receiver' for allosteric inputs from the C-terminus.
results.evaluation: Claims C218-C228 discuss biological relevance with appropriate citations (Frangioni 1992, Brautigan 1993, Krishnan 2014, Choy 2017, Hao 1997, Bandyopadhyay 1997, Rhee 2001, Barr 2009, Villa 2005). The connections to in vivo regulation are reasonable inferences from the structural data and prior literature. However, claims C223-C224 about Tyr152 phosphorylation effects are speculative and require experimental validation.
